newsitem.title: KENYA: Coffee quality, production seen down in Tanzania.
newsitem.headline: Coffee quality, production seen down in Tanzania.

text.p: Coffee quality and production are on the decline in Tanzania and will continue the spiral unless urgent measures are taken by authorities to reverse the trend, researchers in Tanzania said in a report obtained on Tuesday.

"There is going to be an imminent fall in coffee production in Tanzania in the next five to 10 years unless serious efforts are made to revive the industry in the major producing areas," the researchers said in a report dated October 1996.

"Such efforts include seedling production to replace ageing trees, improvement in supply of inputs to farmers, payment of incentive prices to farmers," said the report by leading crop experts A.K. Kashuliza and R.C. Tembele.
Kashuliza is from Tanzania's Sokoine University of Agriculture whereas Tembele is a private consultant.
But Jeremy LeFroy, of the Africa Coffee Co, said Tanzanian coffees were fetching very good prices compared to the world market and continued strong demand was evidence of improved quality.

"The differentials are higher than Colombia or Central America. The only coffee selling higher is Kenya's," LeFroy said. Quality has actually improved. We have not heard a single complaint on quality this year."
The Tanzania Coffee Board has already forecast production will tumble to between 41,000 and 43,000 tonnes in 1996/97 from 53,000 tonnes in 1995/96 and 44,000 tonnes in 1993/94.

The report said declining soil fertility, untimely spraying to combat pests, shortage of labour, inputs and equipment and picking of both under-ripe and over-ripe berries was responsibile for a decline in quality.

"Other problems which have been cited to contribute to the fall in the Tanzanian coffee grade include lack of incentive payment to farmers and the participation of buyers (exporters) in the coffee market," the report said.

"The Ministry of Agriculture and Cooperatives report (1996) observes that whereas with market liberalisation it was expected that the entry of experienced exporters in the coffee buying would revive interest in coffee quality, this has not happened.
"The report accuses the private buyers of pursuing a high market share with little concern for quality of coffee," said the report headlined, "Tanzania Coffee Marketing Study".
LeFroy said that finding was not accurate and the trade association would not want any such traders licensed.

The report added, "Some observers also link this phenomnenon (declining quality) on the haphazard nature with which some of the private traders buy coffee which is not fully dry and mix with good coffee. That would definitely lead to some deterioration in quality."

The report said lower quality was responsible for a decline in prices. It said prices of hard arabicas had eased to 101.79 U.S. cents per kg in 1995/96 from 129.39 in 1994/95 and 156 in 1993/94. Prices of robustas had eased to 100.27 cents per kg in 1995/96 from 129.61 in 1994/95, the report said.
LeFroy said that price chart suggested better prices because world prices had rocketed on Brazilian frost in years stated.

The report said that coffee curing factories had increased to 13 currently from only two since coffee liberalisation was launched. With annual production at an average of 50,000 tonnes, there now was an overcapacity of around 170,000 tonnes.
"Compared to the expected marginal expansion in coffee production, the overcapacity is unlikely to be absorbed in the short or medium term period," the report said.
